Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:54: And now I shall tell you what they said of one of the pious ones. They said that a certain pious man was asked, which day did you rejoice in most, in all your days? He answered: once I was traveling in a ship with merchants carrying fine merchandise, and in order to be alone with my Creator I went down to the back of the ship and lay there in the lowest place - and one of the young merchants arose and disgraced me in his eyes, spat in my face, exposed his nakedness, and urinated on me. I was astonished at his brazenness, but as the LORD lives, my soul was not grieved at all by his deed - and when he passed from my presence I rejoiced with a great joy, that my soul had reached this measure of humility, for I knew from it that it had steps [to climb] among those standing, since it had mastered this attribute to the point that it felt nothing at all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:55: And they, of blessed memory, have already said (see Sotah 5a), that these are the ones who merit resurrection, as it is written (Isaiah 26:19), "awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust" - one who made himself dust in his lifetime. And this is one who does not feel the disgrace of man - and therefore it says, "and My salvation shall be forever."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:56: Now, its saying "who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My law" is not, in my eyes, a mere doubling of the matter, but rather a sign hinting at whom it is speaking to - namely, believers in [divine] providence. And this is because it is known that two men standing to argue before a judge, one does not disgrace the other - and if it does happen so, the insulted one shall be silent and it shall be good in his eyes, since the disgrace of his opponent and the wickedness of his heart shall be revealed before the judge. And therefore it said "who know righteousness" - for he believes in [divine] providence, and that the Master of the whole earth hears the words of the disgracer, and shall repay him his due into his own bosom, and He shall answer on his behalf, and he leaves it to the true Hearer and Examiner of the hearts of men, who knows the matters, whether for good or its opposite - to this point, relevant here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:57: And with these his words we can understand what we say at the end of our prayer, in "my God, guard my tongue from evil," and so on, "and to those who curse my soul, let my soul be silent" - for at first glance it would have sufficed to say "let it be silent," and why "my soul"? And likewise afterward it repeats and says "and let my soul be like dust to all." Rather, the intent is to make known to us that lowliness should be embedded in the soul in such a manner that the soul itself be the silent one - for it is already possible that he not respond to his own disgrace, yet retain hatred stored in his heart, along the lines of (Genesis 27:41), "and Esau harbored a grudge against Jacob, and Esau said in his heart, let the days of mourning for my father draw near," and so on - and Scripture says (Proverbs 16:5), "every proud heart is an abomination to the LORD," even if the pride is in the heart and he does not utter it with his mouth - therefore it said "let my soul be silent," that the soul itself, from its own nature, be silent - and this is like "the people in whose heart is My law," which the pious author, of blessed memory, explained, and like the parable of the man dwelling in a city whose merchants are princes, and so on - and so we explained in the Gate of Love, that all pride and anger come only from the side of matter, for the soul, by its own nature, is lowly before the Creator and before everything, as Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said (Exodus 16:7), "and what are we?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:58: And it said further, "and let my soul be like dust to all" - explaining what it said, "let my soul be silent." How can the soul be silent and not feel it? By already being so accustomed to receiving disgrace, like dust, which is prepared to constantly receive the trampling of people upon it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:59: And the sage, His Honor Rabbi Avraham HaLevi, may his Rock and Redeemer preserve him, said that we should learn the attribute of humility from dust - for dust, as long as it is coarse, is of no use for a craft, and all the more so for making a vessel from it; but the more it is ground fine, the better it is - so too a person. And I say that this is why it said, "and let my soul be like dust to all," for the more he accepts disgrace, the higher his soul shall rise.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:60: And I found that His Honor Rabbi Shlomo Alkabetz, may his Rock and Redeemer preserve him, wrote concerning "and to those who curse my soul, let my soul be silent," an explanation like what I have written. And concerning "and my soul like dust," he wrote: and not this alone, but he shall clothe himself in a garment of humility to the point that he resembles his Maker, whom people sin against, yet He does them good - along the lines of (Nehemiah 9:20), "and You did not withhold Your manna from their mouth" on the day they said, "this is your god, O Israel" (see verse 18, Exodus 32:4) - therefore it said "and my soul like dust to all," for everyone tramples it, yet it raises up for them grain, bread, and food - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:61: And so, along these lines, the pious author mentioned wrote, on the mishnah "be not easily angered" (Avot, chapter 2, mishnah 10) - a fitting explanation on the verse (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "for anger rests in the bosom of fools" - and it corresponds to this teaching, saying that fools, because of the lightness of their anger and their swiftness to anger, anger dwells with them as though it had pitched its tent there - but with the intelligent person it does not "rest," but rather immediately passes. And the meaning of "bosom" is that their anger is hidden and they do not reveal it - to this point, the substance of his words. And this is "and to those who curse my soul, let my soul be silent," as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:62: Further, there he explained another explanation on this verse, along the lines of the explanation of "the people in whose heart is My law" that we have written, and he said, on the mishnah "if I am not for myself, who is for me?" (Avot, chapter 1, mishnah 14), in the name of Rabbi Yosef ibn Shoshan, of blessed memory - and further he wrote that this sage was said of him that he never became angry in his days, and this was so because he never had leisure to become angry at all, being occupied with seeking the life of the soul - and over what should he be angry, when all kinds of anger and rage come over bodily matters? And therefore it said (Isaiah 51:7), "listen to me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is My law; fear not the disgrace of man," as we have already explained - and therefore it said, "anger rests in the bosom of fools," for their heart is hidden from intellect, and therefore it does not rise up to anger. And how noble is their saying, "whoever becomes angry is as though he worships idolatry," which indicates that his thoughts are far from his own essence - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:63: There are further matters fitting to consider so that one not become angry, and we shall explain them in a chapter of their own, in order to give some space between chapter and chapter:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:1: The great cause that prevents anger, hatred, and envy from the heart is when a person considers, in his mind, fulfilling the mitzvah (Leviticus 19:18), "and you shall love your neighbor as yourself," which is a positive commandment including several other mitzvot, as it says in the chapter "Bameh Madlikin" (Shabbat 31a), concerning that convert who came to convert before Hillel and said to him, teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot - and he said to him, "and you shall love your neighbor as yourself" - what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. And when a person considers this, he shall not disgrace his fellow nor insult him, just as he wishes for himself that no one disgrace him - and likewise he shall not respond to his own disgrace, just as, were it the reverse and he were the disgracer, he would not wish to be responded to - and likewise to judge his fellow favorably, and likewise the mitzvot of not taking vengeance and not bearing a grudge, which, when a person fulfills them, he must necessarily overlook wrongs against himself and purify his heart from hatred entirely - behold, by the law of Torah a person is compelled to be humble.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:2: And because love of fellows, distancing from strife, and pursuing peace are the causes that bring a person to humility, I have seen fit to copy here the chapter on "love of fellows" that Rabbi Yisrael, peace be upon him, wrote in his Sefer Menorat HaMaor - these are its words: "you shall not hate your brother in your heart... you shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge," and so on (Leviticus 19:17-18). Our Rabbis taught: "you shall not hate your brother" - one might think he may not strike him or curse him; therefore Scripture says "in your heart" - it is of hatred in the heart that Scripture speaks. And we learn in Tractate Yoma (23a), it is taught: what is vengeance and what is grudge-bearing? Vengeance - he said to him, lend me your sickle; he said, no. The next day his fellow said to him, lend me your axe; he said to him, I will not lend to you, just as you did not lend to me - this is vengeance. And what is grudge-bearing? He said to him, lend me your axe; he said to him, fine - I will not do like you, who did not lend to me - this is grudge-bearing.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:3: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar says, love peace and hate strife - for even idol worshippers, as it were, are not touched by the Shechinah's [judgment] when they are at peace, as it is said (Hosea 4:17), "Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone" - but if there is strife among them, what is said of them? (ibid. 10:2), "their heart is divided; now they shall bear their guilt."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:4: It is taught (see Avot DeRabbi Natan, Zuta, chapter 9): a house in which there is strife is destined to be destroyed, and the Sages say, strife in a city means bloodshed in the city. A synagogue in which there is strife is destined to be destroyed, and some say it is destined to be scattered. Two Torah scholars dwelling in one city, and likewise two courts, and there is strife between them, are destined to die. Abba Shaul says, strife between courts is the destruction of the world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:5: In three places the Holy One, blessed be He, was patient concerning idolatry, but was not patient concerning strife. One: in the days of the generation of Enosh, they began to worship idols, as it is said (Genesis 4:26), "then it was begun to call in the name of the LORD [interpreted as idolatry]" - and He did not exact punishment from them until the generation of the Flood, in which there was strife among them, and they would rob and extort one another - and He was not patient with them, as it is said (ibid. 6:13), "the end of all flesh has come before Me." Second: in the generation of the wilderness, when they made the calf, He forgave them; but when they came to strife, He was not patient with them, for everywhere you find "and they murmured" you find punishment there. And greater than all of these was the strife of Korach, and therefore the Name dealt with Korach and his congregation beyond the letter of the law. Rabbi Berachya said, come and see how severe strife is - for the court below does not punish [capitally] until one is thirteen years and one day old, and the court above until one is twenty - but here even nursing infants perished, as it is said (Numbers 16:29), "if these die the common death of all men," and so on. Third: when the tribes divided over Judah and Benjamin and there was no peace between them, punishment came upon both - when the Ten Tribes sinned, the tribe of Judah came and exacted punishment from them, as it is said (II Chronicles 13:19), "and Aviyah pursued Jeroboam and captured cities from him: Bethel and its villages... and Jeroboam did not retain strength again in the days of Aviyah, and the LORD struck him and he died" - and although Jeroboam worshipped idols and the Holy One, blessed be He, was patient with him, once he divided against the tribe of Judah he was punished.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:6: Rabbi Meir says, strife is severe, for even strife that is for the settling of the world is not called "good" - and in all the account of Creation "good" is said, but in the division of the firmament between waters and waters, "good" is not written of it. And is this not an a fortiori argument? If strife for the settling of the world is not called "good," strife for the destruction of the world - all the more so.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:7: Strife is severe, for it is equal to the generation of the Flood - it is said of Korach's congregation (Numbers 16:2), "leaders of the congregation, summoned to the assembly, men of renown," and it is said of the generation of the Flood (Genesis 6:4), "who were of old, men of renown." Strife is severe, for it brings danger to life, as it is said (ibid. 13:12), "and he pitched his tent as far as Sodom" - because he separated from Abraham, he was close to being destroyed like Sodom, had it not been for the merit of Abraham our father, peace be upon him, as it is said (ibid. 19:29), "and God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot," and so on. Strife is severe, for it brings about death, as it is said (Exodus 21:22), "and if men struggle," and it is written, "and if there is a fatal injury," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:8: Rabbi Yitzchak says, three are called wicked: one who raises his hand against his fellow, one who hardens his face, and one who borrows and does not repay. "One who raises his hand" - from where? As it is said (Exodus 2:13), "and he said to the wicked one, why do you strike your fellow?" - it does not say "you struck," but "why do you strike," teaching that he had not yet struck. "One who hardens his face" - from where? As it is said (Proverbs 21:29), "a wicked man hardens his face." "And one who borrows and does not repay" - from where? As it is said (Psalms 37:21), "the wicked borrows and does not repay." From where do we know that it is forbidden for a person to strike his fellow? As it is said (Deuteronomy 25:3), "forty he shall be struck, he shall not exceed" - and is this not an a fortiori argument? If one liable for lashes, we are commanded not to strike him more than the lashes prescribed, all the more so a person striking his fellow. From where do we know that it is forbidden to provoke one another? As it is said (Deuteronomy 2:19), "and when you draw near opposite the children of Ammon, do not distress them," and so on - and is this not an a fortiori argument? If Ammon and Moab, of whom Scripture said (ibid. 23:7), "you shall not seek their peace or their welfare," it is nevertheless said, "do not distress them and do not provoke them" - Israel toward one another, all the more so.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:9: Severe is hatred, which destroyed the Temple, as we learn in Gittin (55b): "because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, Jerusalem was destroyed," and so on; see there. And there, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said, come and see the power of shame - for the Holy One, blessed be He, assisted Bar Kamtza and destroyed His own House and burned His own Sanctuary.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:10: And because of the sin of baseless hatred Jerusalem was destroyed, and this is hinted at in "how [Eicha] does the city sit alone" (Lamentations 1:1) - the acrostic is EIVAH [enmity]. And we learn in Yoma (9b), it is taught: in the Second Temple, when they were expert and occupied with Torah and acts of kindness, why was it destroyed? Because of the baseless hatred that was among them - to teach you that baseless hatred is equal to idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed. And they, of blessed memory, said there, "for the bed is too short to stretch out on" (Isaiah 28:20) - what is "to stretch out"? From there being two evils [companions] as one [an idiom meaning contradictory things cannot coexist, applied here to hatred among peers].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:11: And most of the suffering that comes upon a person is because of the sin of baseless hatred, as we learn in the chapter "Bameh Madlikin" (Shabbat 32b): it is taught, Rabbi Nechemiah says, because of the sin of baseless hatred, strife comes into a person's household, his wife miscarries, and his sons and daughters die while young.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:12: And we have learned in Avot DeRabbi Natan (see chapter 16, section 1): Rabbi Yehoshua says, an evil eye, the evil inclination, and hatred of creatures drive a person from this world and from the World to Come. For whoever hates his fellow, the Holy One, blessed be He, uproots him from the world - for so we find with the people of Sodom, who were uprooted only because they hated one another, as it is said (Genesis 13:13), "and the men of Sodom were evil," and so on - "evil" to one another, and "sinners" in forbidden relations, "to the LORD" in idolatry, "exceedingly" in bloodshed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:13: And we learn in the Mechilta: "when you see the donkey of your enemy" (Exodus 23:5) - if you subdue your inclination to make your enemy your friend, I promise you that you shall make your enemy your friend, for it is written (Proverbs 16:7), "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him." And the sage said, one enemy should be in your eyes like a thousand thousand thousand enemies, and a thousand thousand thousand friends should be in your eyes like one. And although baseless hatred is a great sin, a person is obligated to hate the wicked just as he is obligated to love the fellows who walk in the straight path, as it is said (Psalms 139:21), "do I not hate those who hate You, LORD?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:14: Another explanation: "when you see the donkey of your enemy" - and if the Torah said this of one who hates him, and so on - all the more so of one who does not hate him. And David, peace be upon him, called the enemy by four disgraceful terms: violence, baseless, false, empty. "Violence," as it is written (Psalms 25:19), "see my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with violent hatred" - these are those who hate the judges who acquit the innocent and convict the guilty, in order to seek out violence [profit through corrupt rulings]. "False," as it is said (ibid. 38:20), "and my enemies are vigorous and strong, and those who hate me falsely are many" - "their deceit is falsehood" (ibid. 119:118) - these are those who hate the upright because they speak truth, while they [the haters] seek to speak falsehood, calling evil good and good evil. "Empty," as it is said (ibid. 25:3), "let the treacherous be ashamed, empty-handed" - these are those who hate Torah scholars, who say there is judgment and there is a Judge, as though it were fitting to say the world is empty [without justice]. "Baseless" - "and words of hatred surrounded me, and they fought me without cause [chinam]" (ibid. 109:3) - these are those who hate their fellows for no reason, as it is said (ibid. 59:5), "without iniquity they run and prepare themselves; awake to meet me, and see."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:15: A person should always love his fellow creatures, and this mitzvah is a positive commandment, as it is said (Leviticus 19:18), "and you shall love your neighbor as yourself." A person is obligated to love his fellow and have compassion on his wealth, as we learn (Avot, chapter 2, mishnah 12): Rabbi Yosei says, let your fellow's money be as dear to you as your own - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained: just as a person looks after his own money, so he should look after his fellow's money, and just as he does not spread a bad name about his own money, so he should not spread a bad name about his fellow's money. If he sees his fellow in a place of danger, he is obligated to save him with all his ability, and if he does not save him, Scripture considers it as though he had killed him, as it is said (Leviticus 19:16), "you shall not stand idly by your fellow's blood" - and they, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 73a), if you see your fellow drowning in a river, or robbers coming upon him, you are obligated to save him, as it is said, "you shall not stand," and so on, and it is written (Proverbs 24:11), "save those taken to death," and so on - and if you say, who sees me? Why should I endanger myself, my own soul is at peace? Therefore Scripture says (ibid. 24:12), "if you say, behold, we did not know this - does not He who weighs hearts understand? And He who guards your soul, does He not know?" - and if he saves him, it is as though he sustained an entire world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:16: And even if he is his enemy or one who hates him, he is obligated to save him, as it is said (Exodus 23:5), "when you see the donkey of your enemy." And whoever does so, the Holy One, blessed be He, is pleased with his deeds, as it is said (Proverbs 16:7), "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways" - meaning, if he desires that the Holy One, blessed be He, be pleased with his way, let him himself repay good to his enemies. How so? If he sees the ox or donkey of his fellow crouching under its burden, he shall help raise it up with him - immediately his enemy shall remove hatred from his heart, and for this the Holy One, blessed be He, shall be pleased with his way. And it is taught, whoever has adversaries above [i.e., in heaven], as we learn (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 10), "whoever is pleasing to people," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:17: A person should always associate with the good and upright, and distance himself from the company of the wicked and worthless people, as we learn (Avot, chapter 1, mishnah 7): Nittai the Arbelite says, distance yourself from a bad neighbor, and do not associate with a wicked person - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Avot DeRabbi Natan 9:1) - whether a neighbor inside the house, or a neighbor outside, or a neighbor in the field - for afflictions come only upon the house of that wicked person, and cause the wall of the righteous person to be demolished too. How so? A wall between a wicked person and a righteous person, and a plague is seen in the wicked person's house - they demolish the righteous person's house because of the wicked person's plague. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, says, woe to the wicked, woe to his neighbor - the wicked person's sins caused the righteous person's wall to be demolished.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:18: Another explanation: "and do not associate with a wicked person" (ibid. 9:4) - a person should not associate with an evil man, for Jehoshaphat associated with Ahab and went up with him to Ramoth-Gilead, and wrath went out against him, as it is said (II Chronicles 19:2), "should you help the wicked," and so on; and again he associated with Achazyahu, and the LORD broke his deeds, as it is said (ibid. 20:37), "because you have associated with Achazyahu, the LORD has broken your deeds." And so we find with Amnon, who associated with Yonadav, who counseled him with evil counsels, as it is said (II Samuel 13:3), "and Amnon had a friend whose name was Yonadav," and so on, and he was wise for wickedness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:19: And we learn in Avot DeRabbi Natan: if the young tell you, build the synagogue, do not listen to them; but if the elders tell you, come let us demolish the synagogue, listen to them - why? Because the building of the young is demolition, and the demolition of the elders is building - proof of this is the counsel of Rehoboam son of Solomon, who abandoned the counsel of the elders and took the counsel of the young.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:20: Do not be a companion to a wicked person, even for matters of Torah, but rather a person should strive to acquire a good companion and distance himself from a bad companion - as we learn in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (chapter 25): "he who walks with the wise shall become wise" (Proverbs 13:20) - to what is this comparable? To one who enters a spice shop: even if he did not give or take anything, he takes away a good scent. So too whoever walks with the righteous takes from their ways and their good deeds. "But a companion of fools shall be harmed" - to what is this comparable? To a person who enters a tannery: even if he did not give or take anything, he takes away a bad odor. So too whoever walks with the wicked takes from their ways and their deeds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:21: The author said, to what is this matter comparable? To two people walking on a road who encountered two groups of people also walking on the road. One group consisted of righteous, upright, God-fearing men - one of the two joined them, and whoever saw him with them thought he was one of them; once they reached the city, he parted from them and entered the city, and they continued on. The second group consisted of worthless men, thieves and murderers, who robbed the possessions of whomever they found on the road - the second man joined them and walked with them, and whoever saw him on the road thought he was one of them; once they reached the city, he parted from them and entered the city, and they went on their way. Two men were coming to the city, and were themselves from that city - the first of them saw the group of righteous men and that man among them, and was telling the people of the city, I saw men on the road, a group of holy, pious men, and I begged them to enter the city so that the people of the city might honor them, but they did not want to; and while he was speaking, behold, that man who had joined them on the road and parted from them near the city was passing by - he said, this man is from that group of righteous men - immediately they gave him great honor and appointed him as their head, all because he had associated with the good. The second man was coming to the city and saw those thieves and robbers - he immediately became terrified and feared for his life and hid until they passed; and once he entered the city, he was telling the people of the city, I saw on the road a band of thieves, and they were killing whomever they found and plundering his money - and while he was speaking, behold, that man who had joined them on the road and parted from them near the city was passing by - he said, this man is from that band of thieves - immediately they seized him and hanged him, all because he had associated with the wicked, even though he had not stolen or plundered with them, and he died a strange death - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:22: And whoever wishes to distance himself from transgressions should distance himself from the company of the wicked - and the sages of ethics said, when you wish to inquire about a person, ask whom he associates with, for every person acts like his fellow's deeds - therefore a person should associate with the good and distance himself from the company of the wicked and the evil. And the sage said, the company of the good is honor and glory, and the company of the vile is disgrace and shame. And whoever associates with the good is like one who carries myrrh: even if he gives none of it to his fellow, he benefits from it; and whoever associates with the wicked is like a person close to a burning furnace: even if he is not burned, he is scorched. And they further said, a person never associates with the wicked and parts from them in peace.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:23: And always, every kind clings to its own kind: the righteous cling to the righteous, and the wicked cling to the wicked, along the lines of (Leviticus 11:15), "every raven after its kind."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:24: And we learn in Bava Kama (92b): people have a saying, a bad palm tree travels and goes to the nest of the sarcha [some bird or bad tree]. Explanation: the bad palm tree, which bears no fruit, associates with barren trees that bear no fruit, and is happy among them. And this matter is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and stated a third time in the Writings. Written in the Torah (Genesis 28:9), "and Esau went to Ishmael." Repeated in the Prophets (Judges 11:3), "and worthless men gathered to Jephthah." And stated a third time in the Writings, "every bird dwells with its own kind, and man with his like" - though this is not found in [canonical] Scripture, but in the Book of Ben Sira, and it said "written" because it is [also elsewhere] written.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:25: And whoever wishes to know his fellow's character should observe what he praises: if he praises good things, it is known that he is a person of good character, and if the opposite, the opposite - and this is what is written (Proverbs 27:21), "the refining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold, and a man is according to his praise" - he praises only according to his own character, whether bad or good.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:26: There are six things a person cannot do, and these are they: one, there is no person who pursues the fulfillment of his desire without sinning. Two, there is no person who constantly converses with women without coming to adultery. Three, there is no person who gathers much wealth without his heart becoming proud over it. Four, there is no person who associates with the wicked and parts from them in peace. Five, there is no person who draws close to kings without the times turning against him. Six, there is no person who requests anything from vile people and has his request fulfilled. And the company of the good is entirely beneficial without harm, even if they give him nothing of their own, and even if they do not intercede on their companions' behalf - even so their company is good and beneficial, since people honor them - and therefore a person should associate with the good. And the sage said, whoever associates with the good, his own level and his family's level shall rise; and whoever associates with the wicked shall eventually become like them, and a wicked man who associates with the righteous shall eventually become like them, as it is said (Proverbs 13:20), "he who walks with the wise shall become wise." And a person should always be a servant to the generous and the good, and not a prince or judge over the light and the lowly, as we learn (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 15), be a tail to lions and not a head to foxes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:27: Rabbi says, when Lot went with Abraham our father, peace be upon him, he learned from his ways and his good deeds - what did Abraham do? He made a lodging house in Charan, and whoever entered he would feed and give drink, and say to him, the God of Abraham our father, peace be upon him, blessed be His Name, is One - and when Lot came [to his own place], he did the same.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:28: And further the sage said, it is not fitting for an intelligent person to associate with a person until he examines whether he is fit for companionship or not. And further he said, companionship is of four kinds: the love of companions resembles food. The first: a person's companionship with his wife and children, as it is said (Proverbs 5:19), "may you always be intoxicated with her love" - and just as a person always needs food, by which his body is sustained, so is a person's companionship with his wife and children always [needed] - just as every single day he needs to see them, and through them he has quiet, tranquility, and settled mind. And from where do we know that a person's wife and children are compared to food? As it is said (Psalms 128:3), "your wife shall be like a fruitful vine in the innermost parts of your house; your children like olive shoots" - he compared the wife and children to a table. The second resembles medicine, and this is the companionship of a brother - for just as a person needs medicine only at a time of illness, so the companionship of a brother is needed only at a time of distress and trouble, as it is said (Proverbs 17:17), "and a brother is born for adversity." The third: the companionship of good friends, and their love and compassion resembles a father's compassion for a son - of a father it is written (Malachi 3:17), "as a man spares his son who serves him," and it is written (Psalms 103:13), "as a father has compassion on his children" - and of a friend it is written (Job 19:21), "have pity on me, have pity on me, you my friends." The fourth resembles a deadly poison, and this is the companionship of the wicked, evil, and worthless people - for just as a deadly poison harms and kills, so such friends harm and kill.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:29: And we learn in the Midrash: whoever associates with a wicked person robs himself of this world and the World to Come; and whoever shows a pleasant face to a wicked person is among those who provoke God; and whoever deceives shall mourn in his own body; and whoever turns his fellow from a good path to an evil path dies in the midst of his days; and whoever mocks the mitzvot receives no mercy from Heaven; and whoever accustoms himself to reddening his fellow's face [with shame], his account is open against him that very day, and so on - as is found in the Pearl of Rabbi Meir, which we copied in the Gate of Fear, chapter 12.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:30: There are fifteen things a good companion must do for his faithful friend, and then his companionship shall be fine and complete without deceit, and these are they: one, he shall greet him first. Two, he must invite his friend to all his good occasions. Three, and on his day of joy. Four, he shall guard his friend's secret and not reveal it. Five, he shall be a helper to him at his time of trouble. Six, he shall visit him in his illness and strive to attend to his needs all the days of his illness. Seven, he shall attend to his burial needs if he dies. Eight, he shall correct his words in his presence, and all the more so not in his presence [i.e., he shall not slander him behind his back, but correct gently to his face]. Nine, he shall overlook all the wrongs his friend committed against him and forgive him immediately. Ten, he shall rebuke him if he knows he has done something improper. Eleven, he shall honor him immediately. Twelve, he shall not deceive him in business dealings. Thirteen, he shall do everything he vowed to do for him. Fourteen, he shall not lie to him. Fifteen, he shall always seek mercy for him and seek his welfare in his heart.
